Really really fun, an absolute must for anyone interested in coding or logic-based puzzle games. Really felt like a challenge for me, as I have very little experience writing in any scripting languages, but it is reasonably easy to pick up and once you get a hang of it, it's smooth as butter. The reasonably low specs needed to run the game also make it ideal as a 'travel game' on non-gaming laptops and such. The writing is fun and pleasant to dig into and I found it very satisfying to read basically everything I got access to, and when it gets serious it is really, really impactful. Many other reviewers have compared it to WatchDogs, and I would agree in some aspects it is similar, however I personally much preferred HACKNET- it felt like all the best parts of WatchDogs for me, which is to say all the weird, quiet side stories bundled into one game. 

However, absolutely cannot recommend to ANYONE with photosensitive conditions (migraines, some people w epilepsy etc.) as it has strobing effects in multiple sequences that were an issue for me- the worst offender (the sequence after you get 'traced') was unplayable for me and I had to exit the program, but luckily I could reload to before the sequence started. The ending sequence does also have this strobing effect, and this is very unfortunate because I could see it preventing people from enjoying the (very good!) ending. As of writing this review I have not played the DLC and thus cannot comment on any strobing lights there.

[b]What's positive (!)[/b]

Hacknet is an exceptionally atmospheric terminal-driven puzzle game that serves as an engaging introduction to fundamental networking and command-line mechanics. Rather than relying on gamified quick-time events, it requires you to interact directly with a Unix-like environment. Navigating directories, manipulating files, and executing core CLI commands such as ls, cd, cat, and scp quickly becomes second nature. Beyond basic shell operations, the game introduces foundational computer science and infrastructure concepts, forcing you to logically chain exploit tools, scan for open standard ports such as FTP on 21, SSH on 22, and HTTP on 80 and target specific running services to compromise root access.

[b]What's negative (!)[/b]

Its primary shortcoming lies in the user interface during late-game network expansion. As the number of target nodes increases, the graphical Display Map degrades in usability due to dynamic node overlap. Selecting specific server locations on the grid becomes increasingly tedious, making manual network mapping and spatial orientation unnecessarily chaotic in the final chapters.

[b]In conlusion (!) [/b]

Despite the cluttered visual map layout in the late game, the combination of realistic terminal interaction and logical sequence planning makes Hacknet a standout recommendation. As a certified IT specialist, I highly recommend it to both tech enthusiasts and prospective Linux admins alike.

It's been some time since I've found a game to be THIS engaging.

I found myself getting into a flow with hopping between nodes, gaining access, looking for details/connections, and removing all of my tracks. It somehow managed to keep my attention for long periods of time--none of which felt wasted.

The characters, despite generally only being portrayed over chat messages/emails/text files, felt surprisingly real, and they all had a unique feel when interacting with them. The DLC is easily the strongest example of this. Hell, even those that you're hacking feel human, as you're looking into their work/personal lives (especially if you're as thorough as I was in looking around)

The main story line is really interesting, and the whole game feels a lot more grounded compared to what you see in many "hacker" games. The side story lines (aka many minor contracts done between main missions) are also very entertaining. They include a lot of miscellaneous files with witty/dumb humor that perfectly portrays how people can be on the internet lol.

The DLC is, in my opinion, just as good as the main game. Things can feel more complex, and there's a lot of interesting things you can find. 

There's also this strong sense of bittersweetness that seems to typify the way main characters exit the scene (aka when you reach the end of their story line), which is only enhanced by the anonymity maintained by all parties. It's kind of insane how personal that feeling can be ([spoiler]hoping for Coel or V to reach back out ;-;[/spoiler]).

Ultimately, if you enjoy sifting through details and uncovering funny and/or interesting story lines while in one of the most well-executed hacker settings, then this game is a MUST. 
As far as I'm concerned, it's an easy 10/10.

SPANDEX IS A PRIVILEGE, BUT THIS TERMINAL IS A BIRTHRIGHT

Yo! Grab your Jolt Cola, slap on your rollerblades, and look at the screen! Look at it!

Most games hand you a plastic neon toy and call it "cyberpunk." Not Hacknet. This isn't some baby-town Hollywood nonsense where mash-keys-to-win happens. This is the digital slipstream!

1. An Elite Adventure: It starts with a dead hacker’s automated distress beacon and spirals into pure, adrenaline-soaked corporate espionage. It’s an actual mystery with real stakes, paranoia, and elite-tier narrative hacking. You aren't just playing; you’re unraveling a digital ghost story.

2. Streamlined for Maximum Rush: Yeah, some commands and mechanics are streamlined so you aren't stuck reading 80-page manual dumps just to crack a port. The pacing moves at lightspeed to keep the thrill alive, but the logic remains authentic and deeply satisfying.

3. Mouse for Casuals, CLI for Gods: You can point-and-click your little desktop GUI like a tourist, or you can live where the legends live: 100% in the command line. Manually hammering out cat, rm *, nmap, and porthack while the system countdown timers bleed red neon makes you feel like you just bypassed the Gibson.

4. Pure Flow State: The soundtrack bumps, the text logs are fascinating to dig through, and when you execute a clean sweep without leaving a single trace, you will want to scream HACK THE PLANET!

It’s smart, thrilling, and an absolute blast of an adventure.

Hacknet is probably one of my favorite lil hacker sims currently, I think it's great fun if you enjoy these types of games!! Downside is you can absolutely softlock yourself quite easy, so make sure to be cautious about what you delete and when, since some important info can be contained in logs or other assorted files. Highly recommended tho!!

Hacknet is largely terminal-based, and is pretty classic for this genre of game: you input various commands and poke around at other systems after hacking into them. There is also a more visual interface you can click around on if navigating purely via terminal is a bit rough for you, but there's a few sections of game that DO require you to only use the terminal, so I'd recommend getting used to it while you can. I come from a coding background so it's hard to say how intelligible this is if you don't have experience messing about with command prompts, but there are some tutorials present so I'm sure you could crack it even if you don't have the experience =)) You'll be digging around inside files for pertinent information, finding ways to mess with said files, delete them outright, or upload your own substitutes in order to complete quests for various factions and progress the story. 

Honestly, I really enjoyed all the hacking puzzles!! I think there's a good mixture of ones that're nice and easy to ease you into it as well as some that felt like they required a bit more digging and clever thinking. The DLC, Labyrinths, was also a pretty cohesive experience but it certainly expected you to have learned quite a bit from the base game so you could work very quickly. The time pressure can be quite real, so I hope you're a fast typer lol.

I ran into one main issue, which was in the DLC. There's a section that asks you to use the command prompt to delete a file, and it seems to be somewhat inconsistent if this works or not - so consider this a brief warning, and a bit of a cheat in case you need it: using your file explorer to delete the file that way seems to work completely fine as long as you have admin. Then validate game files and restart the game and you should be good to go!!

I remember buying this game 10 years ago. I was either 13 or 14 and this game looked awesome, a real "HACK THE WORLD" kind of experience, but in a more realistic light than WatchDogs. When I played it then, it was pretty overwhelming, throwing unfamiliar commands and phrases to my tiny Windows user brain.

It was only when I was around a Junior or Senior in High School that I finally beat the game. It was beautiful, from the badass music to the witty humor hidden in text files; it was a peek into a world I wanted to be a part of.

Immediately after, I began my Computer Science degree in College. I realized that all the phrases the game was throwing at me (SSH, FTP, SMTP etc.) were all real life protocols. It was thanks to this game that I had a head start in my studies, and it was the perfect foundation for my internal computer networking knowledge-base. 

And here I am now, getting my Masters degree in Cyber Security. I use Linux every day, built my own computers and run my own home lab. I've just completed Hacknet, done everything I can do. From Entropy to /el, I've seen everything the base game has to offer.

Would I say it's a realistic hacking simulator? God no, but it's fun and a great entry point for the subject.

TL;DR
My life wouldn't be the same without HackNet.

I have been waiting for the game to start, and now that I'm halfway through I've given up. It's boring and pointless. There is no story, there are no choices (even though the game wants you to think there are). That aside, it's not really a hacking game. "Hacking" just means typing the same commands and waiting for them to execute... every time... for every PC in the network.

Another big problem is that the game implies that it will use real world logic but then it doesn't. Like I can't execute a file on a PC I'm connected to? Since when? 

Instructions are never clear and even if they are I hate that the game forces me to only do things how the dev intended. Specifically for advcancing missions, it's never clear whether I just need to read the file or send it or send the password contained in it. All of those should work, not just one!

There are bugs - mostly soft locks, which is unacceptable for such a simple game.

Instead of spending time on the visualizations for each tool the dev should have spent time designing mechanics around them. For instance the firewall analyzer is okay. Not fun, but it's not completely idle, you have to do something. Each tool has to be like that, there has to be some mini-game associated with it, or there has to be some strategy as to which tools are used in what order.

I don't know what the music was like. It was so repeptitve so annoying I turned it off and played Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines OST. 

The only thing I liked about the game is the environmental storytelling. The chat logs sound EXACTLY like the Old Internet days. Kudos to the author for the research!
